title: Tim Ream’s Important Role in the Growth of American Soccer
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Sophia Vesely8:31 AM EDTTim Ream retired from international soccer last week. / Taylor Banner/USSF/Getty Images The Major League Soccer that Tim Ream left in 2011 to pursue a career in Europe and the one he returned to 13 years later could not have been more different, and neither could he.

“When I left, there were [18] teams,” the 39-year-old Charlotte FC center back tells Sports Illustrated. “When I come back, there’s 30. It has almost doubled in size. Incredible talent throughout the league, coaching, development, everything has just grown so much, and I have as well.”

Ream was a fresh-faced college graduate out of Saint Louis University when he was drafted by Red Bull New York in 2010, back before the existence of any advanced MLS youth pipeline and when college soccer was the primary avenue to keep playing.

Over a decade later, the now former U.S. men’s national team captain and World Cup star was back, having competed at the sport’s highest levels and having laid the foundation of American soccer for generations to come.
A young Tim Ream joined Red Bull New York in 2010. /  Ira Black/Corbis/Getty ImagesIt didn’t take long for Ream to get his footing in MLS.

“When you leave college and get drafted into the MLS, it’s the first step in making a dream come true,” Ream remarks. “As a kid, I dreamed of being a professional soccer player, and that was the first step, and going to a place like New York, it’s like, ‘Wow, this is a little bit daunting.”

If Ream was nervous, it didn’t show. The 24-year-old played every minute of the Red Bulls’ 30 regular season matches his rookie year, leading the team to a club-record 13 shutouts and the top of the Eastern Conference. As a result, he was a finalist for MLS Rookie of the Year. The following season—to be his last in New York, he was once again a constant on the backline, making 28 starts and named to the 2011 MLS All-Star team.

While Ream adjusted seamlessly to the professional game physically, he had a lot to learn about the mental battle and the demands of competing at the highest levels. He discovered that after tough performances, he was presented with just two choices: “You either confront the tough moments head on or you shy away from them and recoil and try to avoid them ... If you confront them, you become a better person and a better player for it.”

Ream was immediately an impact player. / Mike Stobe/Getty Images/New York Red BullsReam credits the Red Bulls’ seasoned veterans, especially former Arsenal legend Thierry Henry who was at the club from 2010 to 2014, for helping him navigate those early moments of his career.
“I played with some unbelievable players, some legends of the game, and being able to learn off of all those guys was one of the biggest and most important times of my early career,” Ream says.

“I paid attention to what guys like Thierry Henry were doing, not just on the field but off the field. How professional they were, how they interacted with everybody, from staff to players to media to fans.”

“It was just the way they carried themselves,” he recalls. “They were confident, but they were also humble ... The Thierry Henrys, the Juan Pablo Ángels, these guys have played in some of the biggest clubs and leagues in the world. Just how much and how hard they worked was an eye-opener for me but a realization of what it takes to compete at that level.”

Ream played for Fulham for nearly a decade. /  Gaspafotos/MB Media/Getty ImagesThose legends of the game ultimately helped Ream make it at the top level.

After two prolific seasons with the Red Bulls, Europe came calling. He transferred to then-English Premier League side Bolton Wanderers at the beginning of 2012, admitting at the time that it was “a hard decision” to leave his MLS community for the Greater Manchester team.

“When you make a move like I did, you do it because you want to challenge yourself, you want to push yourself,” Ream explains. “You learn a lot more about yourself in those challenges, in the hard moments, in the quiet moments that people aren’t seeing.”

After three seasons with Bolton in the EFL Championship, Ream joined Fulham, where he spent the bulk of his club career (2015–2024) and quickly became a local legend. As a mainstay on the Cottagers’ backline, he amassed 312 appearances across nine seasons and helped secure promotion to the Premier League on three occasions (2018, 2020, 2022).

The longevity the man-bun-clad center back had in England proved integral in forging the path for other American players to the European game. Ream joined the likes of legends Brad Friedel (450 Premier League appearances), Tim Howard (399 Premier League) and Clint Dempsey (218 Premier League) as one of the USMNT stars with the most appearances and time spent at soccer’s highest levels overseas.
It is now a path frequently trodden by Americans, seeing current USMNT stars Christian Pulisic, Chris Richards and Weston McKennie, among others, enjoy successful stints across the Atlantic Ocean.
Ream returned to MLS in 2024. /  David Jensen/Getty ImagesBut for Ream, coming back to MLS was inevitable.
